No. Is it an efficient use of an artificial intelligence agent’s time? Also no. But in like three years, the way bond portfolios will work is that some human portfolio manager will call up a robot and briefly describe, in plain English, the characteristics — duration and yield and sector and credit quality and whatever — that she wants in a bond portfolio, and the robot will go out and do the tedious work of finding the right bonds and deciding what to pay for them and negotiating their purchase. And arguably the first step on the path to that future is for the portfolio manager to get an AI agent, and for a dealer bank to get an AI agent, and for the portfolio manager’s bot to connect with the dealer bank’s bot, and for the two bots to negotiate one discrete bond trade within parameters set by humans. We can issue tokens representing ownership of the building, on the blockchain.” I found this very confusing. In fact, for decades, it has been possible to issue shares of a commercial building. It’s traditionally called a “REIT,” a real estate investment trust; most REITs have lots of buildings, but a single-building REIT is possible . There are plenty of REITs listed on US stock exchanges. What did crypto bring to the table? I thought there were three main answers: Technology: Maybe tokens on a blockchain are faster, more efficient, more modern, more 24/7, etc., than shares listed on the stock exchange. Legality: Shares of a REIT — shares of anything, really — are securities under US law, and selling them to the general public requires registration with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, financial statements, disclosure, etc. Many people think this is a good thing — it’s good for investors to know the legally required information about the building they are buying shares in — but crypto people generally thought it was a bad thing, and preferred to avoid SEC registration. Perhaps issuing “tokens” rather than “shares” would avoid the registration requirements. Gambling: It always struck me that, while there was a lot of enthusiasm from crypto founders to tokenize real estate, there was never any obvious enthusiasm from anyone for buying shares of buildings. Did ordinary people want to own some shares in some random commercial buildings? But arguably crypto solved this problem too, simply because in, like, 2021, there was a lot of speculative enthusiasm for owning all sorts of random crypto tokens, which would maybe carry over to owning tokenized real estate. “Tokens always go up, so these real estate tokens will go up, so let’s buy some.” [1] Were these good arguments?
